nameStory: Sesame gets its name from the ancient Greek word 'sesamon,' which traces back even further to Semitic languages where it was called something like 'shamsam.' The plant is also known as 'benne,' a name that came to the American South through enslaved Africans who brought their knowledge of this valuable crop with them.
description: Sesame is an annual herb that grows 2-4 feet tall with a sturdy, upright stem. It's originally from India and is famous worldwide for its oil-rich seeds that give us those nutty sesame seeds we sprinkle on bagels and use in cooking. The plant has simple leaves and produces small tubular flowers that develop into distinctive seed pods that split open when ripe.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive oblong seed pods about 1 inch long that split lengthwise when mature, releasing small flat oval seeds with a rich, nutty aroma when crushed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers, usually white or pale pink, growing singly or in pairs where leaves meet the stem, with a slightly sweet fragrance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Simple oval to lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately on the stem, feeling slightly rough and fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual herb growing 2-4 feet tall with a sturdy, somewhat square stem that's often branched near the top

habitat: Sesame is extremely rare in New England, found only as an occasional garden escape or in community gardens where it's been cultivated. It prefers warm, well-drained soil and full sun, struggling in our cooler climate. You might spot it in urban areas where seeds have scattered from bird feeders or ethnic gardens.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are typically planted after the last frost when soil has warmed, with young seedlings emerging as small fuzzy-leaved plants.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and begin flowering in mid to late summer, with small tubular blooms appearing where leaves meet stems.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods develop and mature in early fall, eventually splitting open to reveal the familiar sesame seeds inside.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely after first frost, leaving only scattered seeds that rarely survive New England winters.

funFact: Sesame pods inspired the famous phrase 'Open Sesame!' from Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves because the ripe pods dramatically pop open with an audible crack, spraying seeds everywhere in a magical-seeming burst.
confusionNotes: The upright growth and simple leaves might be confused with other garden herbs, but the distinctive splitting seed pods and nutty-scented seeds make identification certain once the plant matures.
contextualKnowledge: Though sesame is one of humanity's oldest cultivated crops and drought-tolerant, it's essentially tropical and struggles in New England's climate, making any sighting quite notable for nature observers.
compareHints: Sesame is the only member of its genus you'll encounter in New England, and indeed the only member of the pedal family (Pedaliaceae) in our region. The splitting seed pods and distinctively nutty-scented seeds make it unmistakable among our flora.
